raw_response:
I am a 58-year-old male farmer in Quzhou County. I graduated from the local agricultural technical college forty years ago and have been farming these fields ever since. My family consists of my wife, myself, our son who works in the county town but helps on weekends, and my elderly father who lives with us but no longer works in the fields. I operate 200 mu of land — this is a business farm, not a smallholding. I own a combine harvester, a no-till planter, a rotary tiller, and a sprayer drone. I hire seasonal laborers during peak periods because four people cannot manage 200 mu alone.

It is early April now. The wheat is greening up after winter dormancy, and I am planning the entire season ahead. I have 100 mu under winter wheat that will rotate to summer maize in mid-June. The remaining 100 mu is split: 60 mu for squash and 40 mu for millet. I choose this layout because the processor down the road signed a purchase contract for squash at 1.8 yuan/kg, which is reliable income, while millet is my low-risk reserve crop that stores for two years if prices drop.

For the **winter wheat** on 100 mu: I applied 10 kg N/mu as base fertilizer last October plus 5 kg P₂O₅ and 4 kg K₂O. In late March I already topdressed 8 kg urea-N per mu because the wheat looked a bit yellow after winter — drier than usual. Now at jointing I will apply another 10 kg N/mu, bringing the total to roughly 22 kg N/mu. I will irrigate three times: once now at jointing, once at heading in early May, and once at grain filling in late May. Each irrigation costs about 45 yuan/mu in pumping fees, but at 2.4 yuan/kg for wheat, the return is solid. I expect 500 kg/mu on the better plots, 450 kg/mu average. I budget one herbicide spray and a fungicide at heading to prevent fusarium head blight. Harvest will be around June 10th — I must finish within five days because the maize planting window is tight.

For **summer maize** on the same 100 mu: Immediately after wheat harvest, I will no-till plant hybrid maize — Zhengdan 958 or Denghai series — using my planter-fertilizer combo. Seed costs about 55 yuan/mu. I apply 12 kg N/mu, 4 kg P₂O₅, and 4 kg K₂O at planting, then topdress another 8 kg N at the big-flare stage in late July if rainfall is insufficient. I irrigate twice: right after planting to ensure emergence, and at flowering in early August. Two herbicide applications — pre-emergence atrazine and a post-emergence nicosulfuron if weeds break through. Target yield is 550 kg/mu. The key risk is the one-week turnaround between wheat harvest and maize planting; I hire eight laborers and run my machinery twelve hours a day during that window.

For **squash** on 60 mu: This is my cash crop. I plant hubbard-type winter squash in late April on raised beds with plastic mulch and drip irrigation — I invested in drip tape two years ago and it saves 30% on water. I apply 1,500 kg/mu of composted manure as base (this is my organic matter strategy) plus chemical fertilizer: 15 kg N, 8 kg P₂O₅, and 10 kg K₂O per mu. I split the chemical N: 10 kg at planting, 5 kg at vine running stage. I irrigate four times through the season, timed to fruit set and expansion. Powdery mildew is the main threat, so I budget two fungicide sprays and one insecticide for aphids. Expected yield is 2,500 kg/mu. Labor is intensive at transplanting and harvest — I hire six workers for ten days at each stage.

For **millet** on 40 mu: This goes on the drier, sandier northeast corner where squash would suffer. I plant Jingu 21 in mid-May using saved seed, so seed cost is only 15 yuan/mu. Millet is low-input insurance: 10 kg N/mu as base, 3 kg P₂O₅, minimal K. One irrigation at heading in August if rain fails; otherwise it runs on rainfall. One herbicide at early stage. Expected yield 280 kg/mu. The grain stores in my barn and I sell when prices spike in winter.

Labor planning: my wife and I contribute about 220 family days. Hired labor totals about 190 days — 80 days for the wheat harvest/maize planting crunch, 60 days for squash transplanting and harvest, and the rest scattered across spraying and irrigation. Total input cost this year will run about 92,000 yuan. That is a lot of cash out the door in spring, but I learned forty years ago that under-fertilizing this land costs more in lost yield than the fertilizer itself. I keep a 20,000 yuan reserve for emergencies — I will not drain that to buy more inputs, even if the extension office recommends higher rates. Conservative with cash, aggressive with timing: that is how I have survived four decades of price swings and droughts.
